newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Netanyahu blasts union as Israeli strikes spread.
newsitem.headline: Netanyahu blasts union as Israeli strikes spread.

text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu blasted union leaders on Sunday as a spontaneous general strike shut down large parts of the public sector.
"This is a political, irresponsible and baseless strike," Netanyahu told Israel radio.
"The side that needs to end this is the Histadrut (labour federation)...The country does not belong to them. It's not their private property with which they can do what they want."

The Histadrut called the nationwide strike on Sunday morning following the arrest of trade union leader Shlomo Shani for violating labour court restraining orders in connection with strikes last week.
"When Shlomo Shani is a free man, we will inform all the workers to return to work," Histadrut chairman Amir Peretz told Army Radio.
Union demonstrators gathered and bus drivers briefly blocked roads in front of the Tel Aviv labour court building where police were due to bring Shani for a hearing.
The strike, originally planned for seaports only, spread to airports, the telephone company and state-owned news media in response to Shani's arrest.

A spokesman for the Ports and Railways Authority said Israel's three ports were entirely closed. An Airports Authority spokeswoman said outgoing flights were cancelled and baggage handlers would not transfer luggage of travelers on incoming flights.
Electricity, water and telephone workers went on reduced schedules. Israel's Itim domestic news agency said that court and health workers would also go on strike in the afternoon.
The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange, which the Histadrut said was struck, was still trading. A banks spokeswoman said banks would go on strike on Monday.
The Histadrut began a series of strikes last week to protest against cuts in government spending that union leaders said targetted the poor.
But Netanyahu said the strike was politically motivated. In addition to being Histadrut chairman, Peretz is a member of parliament for the opposition Labour party.
"No one understands why the Histadrut went out on this strike," he told Israel Radio.
Netanyahu said he would consult Finance Minister Dan Meridor on Sunday and perhaps turn to the courts but declined to say what he would do to end the spreading strikes.
Histadrut leaders had said strikes were planned in other sectors in coming days and threatened a general strike when parliament is due to vote on the 1997 budget on Tuesday.

The government's 1997 budget proposal includes seven billion shekels ($2.15 billion) in spending cuts and new taxes and other revenue measures that Netanyahu said are needed to rein in the soaring deficit. Union leaders say the measures will erode workers' salaries.
The budget must pass parliament by the end of the month.
